title: SoccerIQ-Function: Offline Q-Function Evaluation for Estimating Soccer Action Rewards
subtitle: Offline evaluation of long-horizon action value from historical match data
summary: Estimate the long-term value of soccer actions using offline Q-function evaluation with spatial state representations and structured action features.

glance.oneLiner: Offline Q-function evaluation for attributing long-horizon reward to soccer actions.
glance.problem: Action value in soccer is long-horizon and context-dependent, but event-aligned data is noisy and incomplete, making credit assignment and state representation difficult.
glance.approach: Learn an offline Q-function using spatial state tensors (players + ball) and structured action vectors. A CNN encodes the state, an FCNN encodes actions, and a Q-head is trained with shaped possession rewards. We compare TD(0) targets against Monte Carlo returns.
glance.results: TD(0) fits the Bellman equation with low error and generalizes better than Monte Carlo, but qualitative heatmaps still show bias toward safe backward passes. Dribble value surfaces are weak, and data quality limits interpretability.
takeaways: Spatial Q-approximation captures some open-space structure in passing decisions.
TD(0) targets are more stable than Monte Carlo in this noisy offline setting.
Data incompleteness and snapshot noise limit generalization and action nuance.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Modeling soccer is challenging because the game is fluid, strategic, and shaped by many subtle choices. Actions that seem minor in isolation can create goal-scoring chances several steps later, so evaluating long-term value is essential for tactical and player analysis. At the elite level, even small analytical advantages can influence results and transfer decisions, which is why clubs such as FC Barcelona invest heavily in data-driven research.

A core difficulty in applying reinforcement learning to soccer is defining useful state and action representations in a continuous, multi-agent setting. We address this with offline Q-function evaluation, which estimates the expected return of actions taken by the behavior policy using historical data rather than online interaction. We approximate the Q-function with a neural network that combines spatial state images (player and ball positions processed by a CNN) with structured action features (one-hot action type plus continuous targets processed by an FCNN). The resulting embeddings feed a Q-network that predicts expected return for each state-action pair.

sections.title: Approach
paragraphs: We frame offline policy evaluation in soccer as supervised regression on the action-value function $Q^\pi(s,a)$, training a neural network to estimate expected return from historical trajectories. The method has three components: Q-function approximation with different return estimators, structured state/action representations, and possession-based trajectory segmentation with shaped rewards tailored to soccer dynamics.

To estimate $Q^\pi(s,a)$, we learn a neural approximator $\hat{Q}(s,a;\mathbf{w})$ from triplets $(s,a,\text{target})$ by minimizing squared error, $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = (\hat{Q}(s,a;\mathbf{w})-\text{target})^2,$$ optimized with SGD or Adam over offline trajectories from a behavior policy $\pi$. We compare two target choices: Monte Carlo returns, $$G_t=\sum_{k=0}^T \gamma^k R_{t+k+1},$$ which are unbiased but high-variance, and TD(0) targets, $$R_{t+1}+\gamma\hat{Q}(s_{t+1},a_{t+1};\mathbf{w}),$$ which reduce variance at the cost of bias early in training.

State representations adapt SoccerMap-style spatial encodings using a $104\times 68$ grid with four channels: attacker positions, defender positions, and dense distance/angle maps to the ball. Actions combine a discrete one-hot type (“pass,” “dribble,” “shot”) with continuous coordinates: $(x_{\text{start}},y_{\text{start}},x_{\text{end}},y_{\text{end}})$ for passes/dribbles, and only the start location for shots with zeros elsewhere. A CNN encodes the state tensor and an FCNN encodes the action vector; their embeddings are concatenated and fed to the Q-network to predict $Q^\pi(s,a)$.

We define a trajectory as a single uninterrupted possession, starting when a team gains control and ending on loss of possession, a missed shot, or a goal. Because goals are rare, we use shaped terminal rewards to provide denser learning signals: +100 for a goal, +20 for a shot on target, +10 for a shot off target, -10 for losing the ball in the opponent's half, and -20 for losing it in the defending half. This design emphasizes action quality even when goals are infrequent.

sections.title: Numerical Experiments
paragraphs: Experiments were trained on a GTX 4090, and the implementation is available at https://github.com/IgnacioBoero/Soccer.

We use StatsBomb 360 tracking and event data covering 292 matches and over one million events. Events are converted to SPADL format for vectorization, then filtered to passes, dribbles, crosses, and shots. The 360 tracking is derived from broadcast video, which makes it accessible but lower fidelity than 10 Hz tracking; missing players and inconsistent state snapshots are common, and access to higher-resolution data is limited. A compact overview of the model architecture appears in Figure 1.

To minimize distribution shift, we shuffle events across all trajectories and split 80% train / 20% validation. The dataset is sharded and streamed with an iterative loader. Input features are normalized using training-set mean and standard deviation, and target returns are normalized as well.

Regularization includes $\ell_2$ weight decay ($10^{-6}$ to $10^{-3}$), dropout in both encoders and the Q-head ($p_{\text{drop}}$ in $[0,0.20]$), gradient clipping at 1.0, a frozen TD(0) target network updated every 2000 iterations, and early stopping after three epochs without validation improvement.

We run Optuna with 64 trials per method over the grid-search space in Table 1; best configurations and losses are shown in Table 2. TD(0) reaches 0.08 training loss and 0.12 validation loss, while Monte Carlo reaches 0.56 and 0.81, with a larger generalization gap. Losses are not directly comparable across methods because TD(0) measures Bellman consistency, $Q(s,a)-[r+Q(s',a')]$, whereas Monte Carlo regresses to full-return targets. The main limitation is weak generalization, largely due to noisy event snapshots (e.g., player locations misaligned with ball start/end). Beyond loss, inspecting action values for a fixed state provides more meaningful signal.

sections.title: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: Figure 2 shows three examples of model outputs for passing, where the heatmap reflects the predicted reward of passing into each cell. In a mid-block possession state (left), the model highlights the open right flank and downweights the crowded central lane. In a last-phase state just outside the box (middle), it recognizes congestion inside the area and favors space on the periphery. In a build-up state (right), it again flags open wide zones. Across all three, the model assigns high reward to backward passes, which may reflect a learned preference for retaining possession or a bias from the data. Another recurring pattern is lower reward in last-phase contexts, even though optimal decisions near goal should, in theory, be the most valuable; at this point we cannot tell whether this is strategic signal or artifact. During testing, meaningful examples were scarce because many snapshots were incomplete or incoherent, and the model struggled with complex states; richer context consistently produced more interpretable heatmaps.

Figure 3 shows dribble evaluation as a 5m x 5m neighborhood heatmap around the ball. This is the weakest part of the model: the surfaces lack clear guidance about when or where to dribble. We suspect the training data under-represents dribble sequences with high reward, with most positive trajectories coming from pass-to-shot chains, which leaves the model without enough signal to learn coherent dribble value.

The results demonstrate that direct Q-function approximation via deep networks can capture some meaningful spatial patterns in soccer, but also highlight key challenges in data quality, representation, and evaluation. Compared to existing value-based approaches (e.g., VAEP or EPV), our model offers an end-to-end estimate of action values, yet struggles with generalization and nuanced decision-making. Our TD(0) estimator achieved low temporal-difference error on held-out data, indicating successful fitting of the Bellman equation, whereas the Monte Carlo baseline suffered high variance and poorer generalization. The generated pass-reward heatmaps sometimes highlight open space, mirroring SoccerMap's spatial awareness, but also occasionally prioritize backward passes in high-reward scenarios, suggesting the model learned a "safe play" bias rather than true offensive value.

Assuming we had more time and access to a higher-resolution dataset, we would have been interested in further refining our approach. First, we wished we could have conducted a more thorough analysis of our model to determine whether our Q-learning method captured more of the nuances of the game. Additionally, we suspect our approach was highly sensitive to data quality, and we did not allot enough time to clean the data. Finally, we ignored the defensive action space available to the out-of-possession team; analyzing this adjacent but different domain may reveal interesting patterns.
